entries.title: Two lanterns at Old North Church

tiers.kids: On the night of April 18, 1775, two lanterns were hung in the tower of Old North Church in Boston as a warning signal.
tiers.everyday: On the evening of April 18, 1775, two lanterns hung in Old North Church's bell tower warned that British troops were crossing the Charles River toward Lexington and Concord.
tiers.student: On the evening of April 18, 1775, Robert Newman and John Pulling climbed Old North's bell tower and briefly hung two lanterns, a signal from the tallest structure in Boston that British troops were crossing the Charles River and heading toward Lexington and Concord (NPS). Prologue to 1776.

entries.summary: On the evening of April 18, 1775, Robert Newman and John Pulling climbed Old North's bell tower and briefly hung two lanterns, a signal from the tallest structure in Boston that British troops were crossing the Charles River and heading toward Lexington and Concord (NPS). Prologue to 1776.

places.note: Old North Church, Boston (approximate pin).

entries.notes: Era: Founding (1775-1791). Prologue entry (1775), before the section's 1776 start.

entries.title: Declaration of Independence

tiers.kids: In 1776, leaders from the colonies met in Philadelphia and agreed on a letter saying they were a new, free country.
tiers.everyday: On July 4, 1776, the Second Continental Congress approved the Declaration of Independence in Independence Hall, Philadelphia.
tiers.student: On July 4, 1776, the Second Continental Congress approved the text of the Declaration of Independence in the Assembly Room of Independence Hall. The engrossed parchment was not signed that day.
tiers.professional: Approval of the text on July 4, 1776 (Second Continental Congress, Pennsylvania State House) is distinct from the signing of the engrossed copy; the National Archives holds the document as a Milestone Document. NPS finds no evidence that the State House bell (later the Liberty Bell) rang on July 4 or July 8, 1776.

entries.summary: On July 4, 1776, the Second Continental Congress approved the text of the Declaration of Independence in the Assembly Room of Independence Hall. The engrossed parchment was not signed that day.

places.note: Independence Hall, Philadelphia (approximate pin).

entries.title: Surrender at Yorktown

tiers.kids: In 1781, the British army at Yorktown, Virginia, gave up. It was the last big battle of the Revolutionary War.
tiers.everyday: On October 19, 1781, the British garrison at Yorktown marched out and laid down its arms, ending the last major battle of the Revolution.
tiers.student: On October 19, 1781, the British garrison marched to Surrender Field at Yorktown and laid down its arms, ending the last major battle of the Revolutionary War (NPS siege chronology).

entries.summary: On October 19, 1781, the British garrison marched to Surrender Field at Yorktown and laid down its arms, ending the last major battle of the Revolutionary War (NPS siege chronology).

places.note: Surrender Field, Yorktown (approximate pin).

entries.title: Constitution signed

tiers.kids: In 1787, leaders met in Philadelphia all summer and wrote a plan for how the country would be run. It is called the Constitution.
tiers.everyday: On September 17, 1787, delegates in Philadelphia signed the Constitution, a four-page plan that set up the United States government.
tiers.student: Delegates met in the State House (Independence Hall) from May 1787, reached a quorum on May 25, and decided by mid-June to write a new frame of government instead of amending the Articles of Confederation. They signed the four-page Constitution on September 17, 1787.
tiers.professional: The Federal Convention convened May 14, 1787, and worked in closed sessions; chief disputes were central power, representation by state, and how representatives would be chosen (NARA Milestone Documents).

entries.summary: Delegates met in the State House (Independence Hall) from May 1787, reached a quorum on May 25, and decided by mid-June to write a new frame of government instead of amending the Articles of Confederation. They signed the four-page Constitution on September 17, 1787.

places.note: Independence Hall (the State House), Philadelphia (approximate pin).

entries.title: First presidential inauguration

tiers.kids: In 1789, George Washington promised to do his job as the first president, standing on a balcony in New York City.
tiers.everyday: On April 30, 1789, George Washington took the oath as the first president on the balcony of Federal Hall in New York City.
tiers.student: On April 30, 1789, George Washington took the oath of office on the balcony of Federal Hall on Wall Street, then the seat of the new federal government in New York City.

entries.summary: On April 30, 1789, George Washington took the oath of office on the balcony of Federal Hall on Wall Street, then the seat of the new federal government in New York City.

places.note: Federal Hall, Wall Street, New York (approximate pin).

entries.title: Bill of Rights ratified

tiers.kids: In 1791, ten changes were added to the Constitution to protect people's rights. They are called the Bill of Rights.
tiers.everyday: On December 15, 1791, enough states ratified ten amendments to the Constitution. Together they are called the Bill of Rights.
tiers.student: On September 25, 1789, the First Congress proposed 12 amendments to the states. Articles 3 to 12 were ratified by three-fourths of the state legislatures on December 15, 1791, and became the first 10 amendments, the Bill of Rights.

entries.summary: On September 25, 1789, the First Congress proposed 12 amendments to the states. Articles 3 to 12 were ratified by three-fourths of the state legislatures on December 15, 1791, and became the first 10 amendments, the Bill of Rights.

places.note: Ratified by state legislatures; no single place.

entries.title: Louisiana transfer at the Cabildo

tiers.kids: In 1803, the United States bought a huge piece of land called Louisiana. The handover happened in New Orleans.
tiers.everyday: On December 20, 1803, the United States formally took possession of Lower Louisiana in a ceremony at the Cabildo in New Orleans.
tiers.student: On December 20, 1803, in the Cabildo in New Orleans, the United States formally took possession of Lower Louisiana under the Louisiana Purchase Treaty.

entries.summary: On December 20, 1803, in the Cabildo in New Orleans, the United States formally took possession of Lower Louisiana under the Louisiana Purchase Treaty.

places.note: The Cabildo, New Orleans (approximate pin).

entries.title: Winter at Fort Clatsop

tiers.kids: Explorers called the Corps of Discovery crossed the land to the Pacific Ocean. On Christmas 1805 they moved into a small fort for the winter.
tiers.everyday: In November 1805 the Corps of Discovery reached the Pacific. On Christmas Day they moved into Fort Clatsop, their winter camp.
tiers.student: In November 1805 the Corps of Discovery reached the Pacific. On December 25, 1805, they moved into Fort Clatsop, their winter camp on the Oregon side of the Columbia River.

entries.summary: In November 1805 the Corps of Discovery reached the Pacific. On December 25, 1805, they moved into Fort Clatsop, their winter camp on the Oregon side of the Columbia River.

places.note: Fort Clatsop near Astoria (approximate pin).

entries.title: Fort McHenry holds

tiers.kids: In 1814, British ships fired at a fort in Baltimore for a whole day and night. In the morning the fort was still standing and a big flag went up.
tiers.everyday: On the morning of September 14, 1814, after a 25-hour bombardment, Fort McHenry still stood and its large garrison flag was raised.
tiers.student: During the War of 1812, the British bombarded Fort McHenry for about 25 hours. On the morning of September 14, 1814, the fort still stood and the large garrison flag was raised over it, and Baltimore was saved.

entries.summary: During the War of 1812, the British bombarded Fort McHenry for about 25 hours. On the morning of September 14, 1814, the fort still stood and the large garrison flag was raised over it, and Baltimore was saved.

places.note: Fort McHenry, Baltimore (approximate pin).

entries.title: Erie Canal in operation

tiers.kids: Starting in 1825, boats could travel across New York State on a long dug waterway called the Erie Canal.
tiers.everyday: New York's canal system has run since 1825. It helped make New York the nation's main center of trade and opened the interior to settlement.
tiers.student: New York's canal system has been in continuous operation since 1825, longer than any other built transport system in North America (NPS). Population along the route in Syracuse, Rochester and Buffalo quadrupled from 1830 to 1850.

entries.summary: New York's canal system has been in continuous operation since 1825, longer than any other built transport system in North America (NPS). Population along the route in Syracuse, Rochester and Buffalo quadrupled from 1830 to 1850.

places.note: Buffalo, on the canal route (approximate pin; the canal crosses upstate New York).

entries.notes: Era: Expansion and reform (1800-1848). Opening day is [UNKNOWN] in the cited page, so the date is year-only.

entries.title: Cherokee removal (Trail of Tears)

tiers.kids: In 1838, the U.S. Army forced thousands of Cherokee people to leave their homes and move far to the west. Many suffered on the way.
tiers.everyday: In May 1838, U.S. troops and state militia began forcing more than 16,000 Cherokee people from their homelands in the Southeast toward Indian Territory.
tiers.student: In May 1838, U.S. Army troops and state militia forcibly evicted more than 16,000 Cherokee people from homelands in Tennessee, Alabama, North Carolina and Georgia, first to round-up camps and then west to Indian Territory. In June 1838 three detachments left southeastern Tennessee by water (NPS).

entries.summary: In May 1838, U.S. Army troops and state militia forcibly evicted more than 16,000 Cherokee people from homelands in Tennessee, Alabama, North Carolina and Georgia, first to round-up camps and then west to Indian Territory. In June 1838 three detachments left southeastern Tennessee by water (NPS).

places.note: Southeastern Tennessee, where detachments left (approximate area pin; routes crossed several states).

entries.notes: Era: Expansion and reform (1800-1848). Number of deaths is not stated in the cited page excerpt used here: [UNKNOWN] in this entry.

entries.title: Telegraph: What hath God wrought?

tiers.kids: In 1844, a message zipped along a wire from Washington to Baltimore using dots and dashes. It was an early telegraph.
tiers.everyday: On May 24, 1844, Samuel F. B. Morse sent "What hath God wrought?" by electric telegraph from the U.S. Capitol in Washington to Baltimore.
tiers.student: On May 24, 1844, Samuel F. B. Morse sent "What hath God wrought?" from the Supreme Court room in the U.S. Capitol to Alfred Vail in Baltimore. His early system printed raised dots and dashes on paper tape, decoded later by an operator. The Library of Congress holds the tape.

entries.summary: On May 24, 1844, Samuel F. B. Morse sent "What hath God wrought?" from the Supreme Court room in the U.S. Capitol to Alfred Vail in Baltimore. His early system printed raised dots and dashes on paper tape, decoded later by an operator. The Library of Congress holds the tape.

places.note: U.S. Capitol, Washington (approximate pin); received in Baltimore.

entries.title: First Women's Rights Convention

tiers.kids: In 1848, about three hundred people met in Seneca Falls, New York, to say women should have equal rights.
tiers.everyday: On July 19-20, 1848, the First Women's Rights Convention met at the Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls, New York. 100 people signed the Declaration of Sentiments.
tiers.student: The First Women's Rights Convention met at the Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls on July 19 and 20, 1848. About 300 attended, including Lucretia Mott and Frederick Douglass; 68 women and 32 men signed the Declaration of Sentiments (NPS).

entries.summary: The First Women's Rights Convention met at the Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls on July 19 and 20, 1848. About 300 attended, including Lucretia Mott and Frederick Douglass; 68 women and 32 men signed the Declaration of Sentiments (NPS).

places.note: Wesleyan Chapel, Seneca Falls (approximate pin).

entries.title: Gold at Sutter's Mill

tiers.kids: In 1848, a man found gold in a river in California. Soon many people rushed west to look for gold.
tiers.everyday: On January 24, 1848, James Marshall found gold at Sutter's Mill in Coloma, California, starting the Gold Rush.
tiers.student: On January 24, 1848, James Marshall found gold at Sutter's Mill in Coloma, California, the discovery that started the California Gold Rush (California State Parks).

entries.summary: On January 24, 1848, James Marshall found gold at Sutter's Mill in Coloma, California, the discovery that started the California Gold Rush (California State Parks).

places.note: Marshall Gold Discovery site, Coloma (approximate pin).

entries.title: Fort Sumter

tiers.kids: In 1861, soldiers fired cannons at Fort Sumter in South Carolina. This started the Civil War.
tiers.everyday: On April 12, 1861, Confederate batteries opened fire on Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, beginning the Civil War.
tiers.student: On April 12, 1861, Confederate batteries opened fire on the federal garrison at Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, the opening engagement of the Civil War (NPS).

entries.summary: On April 12, 1861, Confederate batteries opened fire on the federal garrison at Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, the opening engagement of the Civil War (NPS).

places.note: Fort Sumter, Charleston Harbor (approximate pin).

entries.title: Emancipation Proclamation

tiers.kids: On January 1, 1863, President Lincoln announced that enslaved people in the states fighting the Union were free.
tiers.everyday: On January 1, 1863, President Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation, declaring enslaved people in the rebelling areas free.
tiers.student: After a preliminary proclamation on September 22, 1862, President Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation on January 1, 1863, declaring that all persons held as slaves within the rebellious areas "are, and henceforward shall be free" (NARA).

entries.summary: After a preliminary proclamation on September 22, 1862, President Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation on January 1, 1863, declaring that all persons held as slaves within the rebellious areas "are, and henceforward shall be free" (NARA).

places.note: "Done at the City of Washington" (approximate city pin; room [UNKNOWN]).

entries.title: Battle of Gettysburg

tiers.kids: For three days in July 1863, a huge battle of the Civil War was fought around the town of Gettysburg, Pennsylvania.
tiers.everyday: From July 1 to 3, 1863, the Battle of Gettysburg was fought in and around Gettysburg, Pennsylvania.
tiers.student: From July 1 to July 3, 1863, Union and Confederate armies fought the Battle of Gettysburg in and around Gettysburg, Pennsylvania (NPS).

entries.summary: From July 1 to July 3, 1863, Union and Confederate armies fought the Battle of Gettysburg in and around Gettysburg, Pennsylvania (NPS).

places.note: Gettysburg battlefield (approximate pin).

entries.title: Surrender at Appomattox Court House

tiers.kids: In April 1865, the main Southern army gave up in a small Virginia village. The Civil War was ending.
tiers.everyday: On April 9, 1865, General Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to General Grant at Appomattox Court House.
tiers.student: On April 9, 1865, General Robert E. Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to General Ulysses S. Grant at the McLean House in the village of Appomattox Court House, Virginia (NPS).

entries.summary: On April 9, 1865, General Robert E. Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to General Ulysses S. Grant at the McLean House in the village of Appomattox Court House, Virginia (NPS).

places.note: McLean House, Appomattox Court House (approximate pin).

entries.title: 13th Amendment ratified

tiers.kids: In 1865, the Constitution was changed to end slavery everywhere in the United States.
tiers.everyday: Passed by Congress on January 31, 1865, and ratified on December 6, 1865, the 13th Amendment abolished slavery in the United States.
tiers.student: The 13th Amendment passed Congress on January 31, 1865, was sent to the states on February 1, and was ratified by three-fourths of the states by December 6, 1865. It provides that neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as punishment for crime, shall exist in the United States (NARA).

entries.summary: The 13th Amendment passed Congress on January 31, 1865, was sent to the states on February 1, and was ratified by three-fourths of the states by December 6, 1865. It provides that neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as punishment for crime, shall exist in the United States (NARA).

places.note: Ratified by state legislatures; no single place.

entries.title: Alaska transfer at Sitka

tiers.kids: In 1867, Russia handed Alaska over to the United States at a ceremony in Sitka.
tiers.everyday: On October 18, 1867, Russian America was formally transferred to the United States at Castle Hill in Sitka.
tiers.student: On October 18, 1867, Russian America was formally transferred to the United States at Castle Hill in Sitka, Alaska; the National Archives holds the Treasury check used for the purchase.

entries.summary: On October 18, 1867, Russian America was formally transferred to the United States at Castle Hill in Sitka, Alaska; the National Archives holds the Treasury check used for the purchase.

places.note: Castle Hill, Sitka (approximate pin).

entries.title: Transcontinental railroad completed

tiers.kids: In 1869, two railroads met in Utah. Now trains could cross the whole country.
tiers.everyday: On May 10, 1869, the Union Pacific and Central Pacific railroads met at Promontory Summit, Utah, completing the first transcontinental railroad.
tiers.student: On May 10, 1869, the Union Pacific and Central Pacific lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah, completing the first transcontinental railroad. NPS notes the four precious-metal spikes honored at the ceremony; their metals and makers are [UNKNOWN] in this entry.

entries.summary: On May 10, 1869, the Union Pacific and Central Pacific lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah, completing the first transcontinental railroad. NPS notes the four precious-metal spikes honored at the ceremony; their metals and makers are [UNKNOWN] in this entry.

places.note: Promontory Summit (approximate pin).

entries.notes: Era: Civil War and Reconstruction (1861-1869). Object angle (ceremonial spikes) is open: needs an official source for each spike's metal and maker.

entries.title: Statue of Liberty dedicated

tiers.kids: In 1886, the Statue of Liberty was opened on an island in New York Harbor.
tiers.everyday: On October 28, 1886, the Statue of Liberty was dedicated on Bedloe's Island, now Liberty Island, in New York Harbor.
tiers.student: On October 28, 1886, the Statue of Liberty was dedicated on Bedloe's Island (renamed Liberty Island) in New York Harbor (NPS chronology).

entries.summary: On October 28, 1886, the Statue of Liberty was dedicated on Bedloe's Island (renamed Liberty Island) in New York Harbor (NPS chronology).

places.note: Liberty Island, New York Harbor (approximate pin).

entries.title: Ellis Island immigration station

tiers.kids: From 1892, millions of people coming to live in America passed through Ellis Island in New York Harbor.
tiers.everyday: From 1892 to 1924, Ellis Island was America's largest immigration station, where over 12 million immigrants were processed.
tiers.student: From 1892 to 1924, Ellis Island was America's largest and most active immigration station; over 12 million immigrants were processed, and inspection took about 3 to 7 hours on average (NPS).

entries.summary: From 1892 to 1924, Ellis Island was America's largest and most active immigration station; over 12 million immigrants were processed, and inspection took about 3 to 7 hours on average (NPS).

places.note: Ellis Island, New York Harbor (approximate pin).

entries.notes: Era: Industry and immigration (1870-1913). Opening day is [UNKNOWN] in the cited page, so the date is year-only.

entries.title: First powered flight

tiers.kids: In 1903, the Wright brothers flew the first powered airplane on a windy beach in North Carolina.
tiers.everyday: On December 17, 1903, the Wright brothers made the first powered, controlled airplane flights at Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina.
tiers.student: On December 17, 1903, Wilbur and Orville Wright made the first powered, controlled airplane flights at Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina (NPS).

entries.summary: On December 17, 1903, Wilbur and Orville Wright made the first powered, controlled airplane flights at Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina (NPS).

places.note: Kill Devil Hills (approximate pin).

entries.title: 19th Amendment certified

tiers.kids: In 1920, the Constitution was changed so that women could vote all across the country.
tiers.everyday: On August 26, 1920, the 19th Amendment was certified: the right to vote could no longer be denied because of sex.
tiers.student: On August 26, 1920, Secretary of State Bainbridge Colby certified the 19th Amendment at the City of Washington; the right to vote could no longer be denied on account of sex (NARA).
tiers.professional: Certification on August 26, 1920 completed adoption nationally. A month later, on September 25, 1920, suffragists gathered on Independence Square in Philadelphia, where the Justice Bell, chained silent since 1915, was rung 48 times, once per state (NPS).

entries.summary: On August 26, 1920, Secretary of State Bainbridge Colby certified the 19th Amendment at the City of Washington; the right to vote could no longer be denied on account of sex (NARA).

places.note: City of Washington; exact building [UNKNOWN]. Approximate records pin at the National Archives.

dates.label: celebration on Independence Square; Justice Bell rung 48 times

entries.title: Stock market crash of 1929

tiers.kids: In October 1929, prices on the stock market in New York fell very fast.
tiers.everyday: On October 29, 1929, U.S. stock prices fell sharply, a day remembered as Black Tuesday.
tiers.student: On October 29, 1929, U.S. stock prices fell sharply in a session remembered as Black Tuesday (Federal Reserve History).

entries.summary: On October 29, 1929, U.S. stock prices fell sharply in a session remembered as Black Tuesday (Federal Reserve History).

places.note: New York Stock Exchange area (approximate pin).

entries.title: Social Security Act

tiers.kids: In 1935, a new law started Social Security, to help older people and others who needed support.
tiers.everyday: On August 14, 1935, the Social Security Act was approved, creating federal old-age benefits and grants to states.
tiers.student: Approved on August 14, 1935, the Social Security Act set up a system of federal old-age benefits, grants to states for old-age assistance, unemployment compensation administration and aid to dependent children, and a Social Security Board (SSA archival text).

entries.summary: Approved on August 14, 1935, the Social Security Act set up a system of federal old-age benefits, grants to states for old-age assistance, unemployment compensation administration and aid to dependent children, and a Social Security Board (SSA archival text).

tiers.everyday: On September 30, 1935, President Franklin D. Roosevelt dedicated Boulder Dam, now Hoover Dam, on the Colorado River.
tiers.student: On September 30, 1935, President Franklin D. Roosevelt dedicated Boulder Dam (now Hoover Dam) on the Colorado River; NPS Teaching with Historic Places confirms its 1935 completion.

entries.summary: On September 30, 1935, President Franklin D. Roosevelt dedicated Boulder Dam (now Hoover Dam) on the Colorado River; NPS Teaching with Historic Places confirms its 1935 completion.

places.note: Hoover Dam on the Colorado River, NV/AZ line (approximate pin).

entries.title: Attack on Pearl Harbor

tiers.kids: On December 7, 1941, Japanese planes attacked U.S. ships at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii.
tiers.everyday: On December 7, 1941, the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor struck the U.S. Pacific Fleet in Hawaii.
tiers.student: On December 7, 1941, the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor struck the U.S. Pacific Fleet in Hawaii (NPS).

entries.summary: On December 7, 1941, the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor struck the U.S. Pacific Fleet in Hawaii (NPS).

places.note: USS Arizona Memorial area, Pearl Harbor (approximate pin).

entries.title: United Nations Charter signed

tiers.kids: In 1945, countries met in San Francisco and signed a plan to work for peace together: the United Nations.
tiers.everyday: On June 26, 1945, delegates in San Francisco signed the Charter of the United Nations.
tiers.student: On June 26, 1945, delegates at the San Francisco conference signed the Charter of the United Nations (State Department Office of the Historian).

entries.summary: On June 26, 1945, delegates at the San Francisco conference signed the Charter of the United Nations (State Department Office of the Historian).

places.note: War Memorial Veterans Building, San Francisco (approximate pin; exact hall [UNKNOWN]).

entries.title: Brown v. Board of Education

tiers.kids: In 1954, the Supreme Court said it was wrong to keep Black and white children in separate public schools.
tiers.everyday: On May 17, 1954, the Supreme Court ruled in Brown v. Board of Education that racial segregation in public schools was unconstitutional.
tiers.student: On May 17, 1954, the Supreme Court decided Brown v. Board of Education, ruling that separating children in public schools on the basis of race was unconstitutional and overruling the "separate but equal" principle of Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) (NARA).

entries.summary: On May 17, 1954, the Supreme Court decided Brown v. Board of Education, ruling that separating children in public schools on the basis of race was unconstitutional and overruling the "separate but equal" principle of Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) (NARA).

places.note: Supreme Court of the United States (approximate pin).

entries.title: Little Rock Central High School

tiers.kids: In 1957, nine Black students went to an all-white high school in Little Rock, Arkansas, protected by soldiers.
tiers.everyday: On September 25, 1957, the Little Rock Nine entered Central High School under the escort of federal troops.
tiers.student: On September 25, 1957, nine Black students, the Little Rock Nine, entered Central High School in Little Rock under escort of federal troops (NPS).

entries.summary: On September 25, 1957, nine Black students, the Little Rock Nine, entered Central High School in Little Rock under escort of federal troops (NPS).

places.note: Little Rock Central High School (approximate pin).

entries.title: March on Washington

tiers.kids: In 1963, a huge crowd gathered at the Lincoln Memorial to ask for jobs and freedom for all.
tiers.everyday: On August 28, 1963, the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom gathered at the Lincoln Memorial.
tiers.student: On August 28, 1963, the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom gathered at the Lincoln Memorial, where Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his "I Have a Dream" speech (NPS).

entries.summary: On August 28, 1963, the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom gathered at the Lincoln Memorial, where Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his "I Have a Dream" speech (NPS).

entries.title: Civil Rights Act of 1964

tiers.kids: In 1964, a new law said businesses and public places could not treat people unfairly because of their race.
tiers.everyday: On July 2, 1964, the Civil Rights Act became law. It outlawed segregation in public places and banned job discrimination.
tiers.student: Signed on July 2, 1964, the Civil Rights Act prohibited discrimination in public places, provided for integration of schools and other public facilities, and made employment discrimination illegal; NARA calls it the most sweeping civil rights legislation since Reconstruction.

entries.summary: Signed on July 2, 1964, the Civil Rights Act prohibited discrimination in public places, provided for integration of schools and other public facilities, and made employment discrimination illegal; NARA calls it the most sweeping civil rights legislation since Reconstruction.

entries.title: Edmund Pettus Bridge, Selma

tiers.kids: In 1965, people marching for the right to vote were attacked on a bridge in Selma, Alabama.
tiers.everyday: On March 7, 1965, voting-rights marchers were attacked on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, a day remembered as Bloody Sunday.
tiers.student: On March 7, 1965, voting-rights marchers were attacked on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama, a day remembered as Bloody Sunday; the later Selma-to-Montgomery march followed (NPS).

entries.summary: On March 7, 1965, voting-rights marchers were attacked on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama, a day remembered as Bloody Sunday; the later Selma-to-Montgomery march followed (NPS).

places.note: Edmund Pettus Bridge, Selma (approximate pin).

entries.title: Apollo 11

tiers.kids: In July 1969, a rocket launched from Florida and carried astronauts to the Moon. They landed on July 20.
tiers.everyday: On July 16, 1969, Apollo 11 lifted off from Kennedy Space Center. The lunar landing followed on July 20.
tiers.student: Apollo 11 lifted off from Launch Complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center on July 16, 1969, and landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969 (NASA).

entries.title: Mount St. Helens erupts

tiers.kids: In 1980, a volcano in Washington State blew up and its side collapsed.
tiers.everyday: On May 18, 1980, Mount St. Helens erupted in a cataclysmic blast that collapsed the north flank of the volcano.
tiers.student: On May 18, 1980, Mount St. Helens erupted in a cataclysmic blast that collapsed the north flank of the volcano (USGS).

entries.title: Americans with Disabilities Act

tiers.kids: In 1990, a law was signed to make sure people with disabilities are treated fairly at work, at school and in public places.
tiers.everyday: Signed on July 26, 1990, the Americans with Disabilities Act was a comprehensive civil rights law for people with disabilities.

entries.title: September 11, 2001

tiers.kids: On September 11, 2001, terrorists attacked the United States. Many people died. One plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania.
tiers.everyday: On September 11, 2001, attacks struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, and United Flight 93 crashed near Shanksville, Pennsylvania.
tiers.student: On September 11, 2001, United Airlines Flight 93 crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania; attacks that morning also struck the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon (NPS).

entries.title: COVID-19 pandemic in the United States

tiers.kids: In 2020, a new illness called COVID-19 spread around the world, and life changed in the United States.
tiers.everyday: On January 20, 2020, CDC reported the first lab-confirmed U.S. case of the new coronavirus, from Washington state. On March 11, 2020, WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic.
tiers.student: CDC reported the first laboratory-confirmed U.S. case of the 2019 novel coronavirus on January 20, 2020, from samples taken January 18 in Snohomish County, Washington, and activated its Emergency Operations Center. On March 11, 2020, WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic (CDC Museum timeline).
